truth.text: In 1932, the Australian military deployed soldiers with Lewis machine guns against 20,000 emus—and the emus won.
facts: WWI veterans farming Western Australia lost wheat to migrating emus
Major Meredith led two soldiers with two Lewis machine guns
Emus split into small groups and outran the gun trucks
After ~10,000 rounds and a month, the army withdrew

lies.text: In 1941, the British Army trained a unit of carrier pigeons to drop small smoke bombs over German tank columns.
facts: Britain's National Pigeon Service supplied about 250,000 birds in WWII
Homing pigeons fly back to their home loft, often 100+ miles
Smoke grenades hide troop movements from enemy view

truth.text: In 1925, Greece and Bulgaria fought a border war that was triggered when a Greek soldier chased his runaway dog across the border.
facts: Tensions were already high on the Greek–Bulgarian border
Bulgarian sentries shot the soldier as he crossed after his dog
Greece invaded, demanding an apology and compensation
League of Nations ordered a ceasefire; Greece paid £45,000

lies.text: In 1899, a brief military skirmish between Belgium and the Netherlands erupted over a herd of escaped sheep that ate a border post.
facts: Belgium broke away from the Netherlands in the 1830 revolution
Their border has odd enclaves, like Baarle-Hertog
Border posts were stone or iron markers along the line

truth.text: The Netherlands and the Isles of Scilly were officially at war for 335 years from 1651 to 1986 without a single shot ever fired.
facts: Dutch declared war after Royalist ships on Scilly raided Dutch shipping
Royalists surrendered to Parliament months later, before any fighting
No peace treaty was signed, so the war technically continued
A local historian asked the Dutch embassy; peace signed April 1986

lies.text: Spain and Portugal were technically at war for 180 years because a 1668 peace treaty was never ratified by the Spanish court.
facts: Portugal won independence from Spain in the Restoration War, 1640–1668
The 1668 Treaty of Lisbon ended that war
Ratification is a ruler formally approving a treaty

truth.text: In 1518, hundreds of citizens in Strasbourg danced uncontrollably in the streets for weeks until many collapsed from exhaustion.
facts: Began when a woman, Frau Troffea, danced alone for days
The region was suffering famine and disease
Officials thought more dancing would cure it, so hired musicians
Some died of exhaustion; survivors were taken to a St. Vitus shrine

lies.text: In 1642, an entire Bavarian town was struck by a mass laughing fit that lasted nearly two months.
facts: Laughter spreads easily through groups
Mass psychogenic illness spreads symptoms without a physical cause
Bavaria in 1642 was ravaged by the Thirty Years' War

truth.text: In 897 AD, Pope Stephen VI had the rotting corpse of his predecessor exhumed, dressed in papal robes, and placed on trial.
facts: The dead pope, Formosus, had crowned a rival of Stephen's backers
Stephen wanted Formosus's acts and ordinations declared invalid
A deacon stood beside the corpse to answer for it
Found guilty; blessing fingers cut off, body thrown in the Tiber
Public outrage got Stephen jailed and strangled months later

lies.text: In 1345, the King of Bohemia appointed his favorite wolfhound an honorary member of the royal council.
facts: Wolfhounds are giant hunting dogs prized by medieval nobles
A royal council advised the king on law, war and taxes
Bohemia was a kingdom in today's Czech Republic, ruled from Prague
King John of Bohemia ruled from 1310 to 1346

truth.text: A French entertainer known as 'Monsieur Mangetout' ate an entire Cessna 150 airplane piece by piece over two years.
facts: His real name was Michel Lotito
French entertainer who ate metal and glass from childhood
He had pica and an unusually thick stomach lining
Ate about 1 kg of metal a day, cut into small pieces
Also ate bicycles, TVs and a coffin

lies.text: A Belgian contortionist lived inside a 1968 Volkswagen Beetle for 14 months as a protest performance.
facts: The VW Beetle seats four and is about 4 meters long
Contortionists train extreme flexibility, often from childhood
Endurance artists like Tehching Hsieh did year-long performances

truth.text: An American farmer hiccuped continuously for 68 years from 1922 to 1990.
facts: His name was Charles Osborne
Began in 1922 while he lifted a 350-pound hog
Likely damage to the brain area that controls hiccups
Up to 40 hiccups a minute, later slowing to 20
Married twice with eight children; stopped in 1990, died 1991

lies.text: A Scottish bagpipe player sneezed roughly every 15 minutes for 22 years due to a rare nerve condition.
facts: A sneeze is a reflex triggered through the trigeminal nerve
Bagpipes need steady breath pressure fed into a bag
Guinness tracks medical oddities like the longest sneezing fit

truth.text: A single lightning megaflash in North America spanned a continuous distance of 477 miles across three US states.
facts: Happened on April 29, 2020
Megaflashes spread sideways through huge storm systems
Crossed Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi
Measured by weather satellites, confirmed by the WMO

lies.text: In 1997, a single thunderstorm over Kansas produced continuous lightning for 41 hours without a single pause.
facts: Some regions see lightning on most nights of the year
Supercells are long-lived rotating thunderstorms
Kansas sits in the Great Plains storm belt

truth.text: The longest continuous game of Monopoly ever officially recorded lasted for 70 straight days (1,680 hours).
facts: The record claim comes from Hasbro, Monopoly's maker
Monopoly grew out of The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904
Other marathon games were played in bathtubs and underwater
House rules like Free Parking cash make games drag on

lies.text: Two Russian chess grandmasters once played a single game of chess that lasted uninterrupted for 18 days in an underground bunker.
facts: Tournament chess uses clocks that cap each player's thinking time
Draw rules end games after repeated moves
Grandmaster is chess's top lifetime title

truth.text: The Texas horned lizard can shoot pressurized streams of foul blood directly from its eye sockets up to five feet.
facts: Squirts mainly at dogs, coyotes and other canines
It raises blood pressure in its head until vessels burst
The blood tastes awful to canines, maybe from ants it eats
Texas's state reptile, nicknamed the 'horny toad'

lies.text: The Himalayan snow owl can rotate its head a full 360 degrees thanks to an extra vertebra in its neck.
facts: Owls have 14 neck vertebrae; humans have 7
Owl eyes are fixed tubes, so the head must turn instead
Snowy owls live on the Arctic tundra

truth.text: The jellyfish Turritopsis dohrnii can revert its mature adult cells back to their earliest polyp stage, achieving biological immortality.
facts: A tiny jellyfish, about 4.5 mm across
When stressed, it shrinks into a blob, then regrows as a polyp
The cell change is called transdifferentiation
It can still die from predators or disease

lies.text: The Greenland deep-sea sponge can freeze solid in winter and resume feeding normally when it thaws in spring.
facts: Sponges are simple animals that filter food from seawater
Deep water off Greenland stays just above freezing
Some insects survive freezing using antifreeze proteins

truth.text: Bombardier beetles mix hydroquinone and hydrogen peroxide in an internal chamber to blast boiling caustic chemicals at 100°C from their abdomens.
facts: Defends against ants, frogs and birds
Enzymes trigger an explosive reaction in a hardened chamber
The spray pops out at about 100°C
Fires in rapid pulses, around 500 a second

lies.text: The Amazonian trapdoor spider seals its burrow with a door made of its own shed skin that it glues shut with saliva.
facts: Trapdoor spiders hide in burrows under hinged lids
Spiders molt, shedding their exoskeleton as they grow
They ambush prey that walks past the burrow

truth.text: Male platypuses have sharp venomous calcaneus spurs on their hind ankles capable of causing agonizing pain that resists morphine.
facts: Only males have venom, used to fight rival males
Venom glands swell during breeding season
Not lethal to humans, but pain can last weeks
Even morphine barely dulls the pain

lies.text: The platypus can stay underwater for up to two hours by slowing its heart to just three beats per minute.
facts: Platypuses hunt with electroreceptors in their bills
They close their eyes, ears and nose underwater
Diving mammals slow their heart rate to save oxygen

truth.text: Wombats are the only known animal species on Earth that produce distinctly cube-shaped feces.
facts: Cubes form in the gut's last stretch, where wall stiffness varies
Wombats stack them on rocks and logs to mark territory
Slow digestion, up to two weeks, makes them dry and firm
The research won a 2019 Ig Nobel Prize

lies.text: Koalas store undigested eucalyptus leaves in a cheek pouch to snack on during cold nights.
facts: Koalas eat almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves
Eucalyptus is low-energy, so koalas sleep up to 20 hours
Hamsters and some monkeys really have cheek pouches

truth.text: Soviet and Russian cosmonauts carried a three-barreled shotgun called the TP-82 into space on missions until 2006.
facts: Why: Voskhod 2 landed far off course in Siberian forest in 1965
Leonov and Belyayev waited in the cold among wolves and bears
Fired shot, rifle and flare rounds; the stock held a machete
Kept in Soyuz survival kits until 2006

lies.text: Yuri Gagarin secretly carried a small canary feather sewn into his spacesuit glove as a good-luck charm.
facts: Gagarin flew Vostok 1 on April 12, 1961
His flight lasted 108 minutes, one orbit
Cosmonauts keep rituals, like watching a set film before launch

truth.text: Hundreds of trees growing across Earth today were grown from seeds that orbited the Moon during the Apollo 14 mission.
facts: Astronaut Stuart Roosa was a former Forest Service smokejumper
He carried ~500 seeds in his personal kit for the Forest Service
Species: loblolly pine, sycamore, sweetgum, redwood, Douglas fir
Many were planted for the 1976 US bicentennial

lies.text: Apollo 12 astronauts left a sealed container of moss spores on the lunar surface to test survival.
facts: Apollo 12 landed in November 1969, the second Moon landing
Moss spores can survive extreme cold and dryness
Apollo crews left experiment packages called ALSEP on the Moon

truth.text: Astronauts returning from spacewalks consistently report that outer space smells like seared steak, hot metal, and welding fumes.
facts: Noticed when the airlock repressurizes after a spacewalk
The odor clings to suits, helmets and tools
Likely from atomic oxygen reacting with surfaces
NASA had a chemist recreate it for training

lies.text: Astronauts report that the inside of the International Space Station smells strongly of cinnamon because of a cleaning product.
facts: The ISS has been continuously crewed since November 2000
Station air is scrubbed by filters and CO2 removal systems
NASA tests materials so they don't give off strong smells

truth.text: A portion of a famous planetary scientist's cremated ashes was buried on the Moon by the Lunar Prospector spacecraft.
facts: Shoemaker co-discovered comet Shoemaker–Levy 9
He trained Apollo astronauts in geology
He dreamed of going to the Moon, but a health condition grounded him
Died in a 1997 car crash; his ashes reached the Moon in 1999

lies.text: In 1999, NASA's Mars Polar Lander secretly carried a capsule of its project manager's ashes toward the Martian south pole.
facts: Mars Polar Lander launched in January 1999
It lost contact during its landing in December 1999
Companies like Celestis launch cremated remains into space

truth.text: In 1994, a 17-year-old Michigan Boy Scout tried to build a nuclear breeder reactor in his backyard shed, and the EPA had to clean up the site.
facts: David Hahn had earned the Atomic Energy merit badge
Took americium from smoke detectors, thorium from lantern mantles
Caught in 1994 when police searched his car
EPA cleanup cost about $60,000; shed parts buried in Utah

lies.text: In 1982, an Ohio high school student built a working jet engine in his garage and mounted it on a bicycle.
facts: Pulse jets are simple jet engines hobbyists can build
A jet engine needs fuel, compressed air and ignition

truth.text: An experiment started in 1927 in Queensland to prove pitch is a liquid has only dropped nine drips of tar in nearly a century.
facts: Physicist Thomas Parnell set it up to show pitch flows
Pitch is roughly 100 billion times thicker than water
A drop falls about once a decade
Nobody has seen one fall live; a camera failed in 2000

lies.text: A Cambridge lab has kept a candle burning inside a sealed jar since 1903 to test oxygen recycling.
facts: A candle flame goes out once it uses up the oxygen
Cambridge's Cavendish Laboratory dates from 1874
Sealed bottle gardens can recycle their air for decades

truth.text: An experimental battery-powered bell at Oxford University has been ringing continuously since 1840—over 180 years.
facts: Set up in 1840 by Rev. Robert Walker
A tiny ball shuttles between two bells, pushed by static charge
Sealed under glass, so it's nearly silent
Nobody opens it, fearing the batteries would be ruined

lies.text: An Oxford physics lab has kept a sealed jar of honey crystallizing undisturbed since 1888 as a viscosity experiment.
facts: Honey crystallizes as glucose separates out
Viscosity measures how thick and slow a fluid flows
Honey is mostly fructose and glucose

truth.text: Under specific thermodynamic conditions, hot water can freeze faster than cold water—a phenomenon known as the Mpemba Effect.
facts: Named after Tanzanian student Erasto Mpemba
His hot ice-cream mix froze before the cold one
Physicist Denis Osborne tested it with him and published in 1969
Possible causes: evaporation, convection, dissolved gases

lies.text: Water containing a pinch of salt freezes about twice as fast as pure water in a home freezer.
facts: Home freezers sit around −18°C (0°F)
Supercooled water can stay liquid below 0°C
Ice-cream makers use salt with ice to chill the mix

truth.text: In 1814, a 22-foot-tall wooden vat burst at a London brewery, unleashing a 15-foot tidal wave of fermented beer that leveled buildings.
facts: At Meux's Horse Shoe Brewery, near Tottenham Court Road
An iron hoop had slipped off the vat an hour earlier
The wave burst other vats, flooding a poor neighborhood

lies.text: In 1928, a burst fermentation tank flooded a Munich street with dark lager up to the ankles.
facts: Lager ferments cold in large tanks
Munich is home to Oktoberfest and big breweries
Germany's 1516 purity law limited beer ingredients

truth.text: In 1970, the Oregon Highway Division tried to dispose of a dead 45-foot sperm whale using a half-ton of dynamite, raining blubber across the town.
facts: Happened in November 1970 at Florence, Oregon
Burying or burning it seemed too hard
They hoped seagulls would eat the small pieces
Blubber rained on onlookers; most of the whale stayed put

lies.text: In 1984, Seattle officials tried to sink a derelict barge by filling it with sand from a helicopter.
facts: Derelict vessels are abandoned boats, costly to remove
Ships are usually scuttled by flooding or explosives
Heavy-lift helicopters can carry around 10 tons

truth.text: In 1919, a steel tank collapsed in Boston, releasing a 25-foot wave of sticky molasses traveling at 35 mph that killed 21 people.
facts: Purity Distilling stored molasses to make industrial alcohol
The tank was badly built and leaked
A sudden warm spell raised pressure inside
21 died, 150 hurt; it led to stricter building rules

lies.text: In 1876, a collapsed vinegar silo in Bristol flooded several streets with acidic runoff.
facts: Vinegar is about 5% acetic acid
Bristol was a major British port and industrial city
Silos store bulk grain or liquids

truth.text: Castoreum, a compound secreted from the anal scent glands of beavers, was historically used as natural vanilla and raspberry flavoring.
facts: Beavers use it to mark territory
Collected from scent sacs under the beaver's tail
Its vanilla-like scent comes from the bark they eat
Also used in perfume; rare in food now because it's costly

lies.text: Early natural banana flavoring was distilled from the skins of rotting apples.
facts: Artificial banana flavor is mostly isoamyl acetate
Isoamyl acetate forms naturally in ripening fruit
Older flavorings were extracted from plant and animal sources

truth.text: Casu Marzu is a traditional Sardinian sheep milk cheese deliberately infested with thousands of live, jumping insect maggots.
facts: Cheese flies lay eggs in cut-open pecorino
The larvae digest fats, making it soft and pungent
Larvae can jump about 15 cm, so eaters shield their eyes
Banned under EU food rules but still eaten locally

lies.text: A traditional Normandy cheese is aged in wooden boxes lined with beeswax and dried lavender.
facts: Normandy makes Camembert, Livarot and Pont-l'Évêque
Camembert is traditionally sold in round wooden boxes
Lavender grows mainly in Provence, in southern France

truth.text: Eating the berry of the Miracle Fruit plant contains a protein called miraculin that makes intensely sour lemons taste like sweet lemonade.
facts: The plant is Synsepalum dulcificum, from West Africa
Miraculin binds to the tongue's sweet receptors
Acids switch it on, so sour things taste sweet
The effect lasts 30 to 60 minutes

lies.text: Chewing raw ginger before eating makes salty foods taste sweet for about 20 minutes.
facts: Ginger's heat comes from compounds called gingerols
Taste buds detect sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami
Some foods really alter taste, like artichokes

truth.text: Cotton candy (originally called 'Fairy Floss') was co-invented in 1897 by a practicing dentist.
facts: Morrison was a dentist in Nashville
His partner was confectioner John C. Wharton
Their machine spun melted sugar through tiny holes
They sold 68,000 boxes at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair

lies.text: The original cotton candy flavor was formulated using vanilla extract and rose water.
facts: Cotton candy is spun from threads of melted sugar
Rose water flavors sweets like Turkish delight
Vanilla extract was made commercially by the 1800s

truth.text: Between 2011 and 2012, thieves stole 3,000 tons of maple syrup worth $18 million from Quebec's global strategic reserve.
facts: Quebec keeps a syrup reserve to stabilize prices
The thieves rented space in the same warehouse
They siphoned syrup and refilled barrels with water
Caught during an inventory; the mastermind got eight years

lies.text: In 2008, thieves in Switzerland stole 45 tons of chocolate from a Lindt warehouse using stolen delivery trucks.
facts: Lindt is a Swiss chocolate maker founded in 1845
Cargo thieves often pose as legitimate carriers
A truck trailer holds roughly 20 tons

truth.text: In 2009, an American flute student broke into a British natural history museum and stole 299 rare bird skins to sell for salmon fishing flies.
facts: Edwin Rist was a 20-year-old flute student
Victorian fly-tying uses rare exotic feathers
He broke in through a window at night
Many skins were collected by Alfred Russel Wallace

lies.text: In 1999, a burglar stole a jeweled scepter from a London museum by hiding inside a display case overnight.
facts: The Crown Jewels are kept in the Tower of London
Many museums hold royal regalia like scepters
Thomas Blood tried to steal the Crown Jewels in 1671

truth.text: In 1995, a bank robber in Pittsburgh robbed two banks with no disguise after rubbing lemon juice on his face believing it made him invisible to cameras.
facts: McArthur Wheeler robbed two Pittsburgh banks
Lemon juice works as invisible ink, so he thought it hid him
A test Polaroid came out blank, convincing him

Inspired the Dunning–Kruger study

lies.text: In 2002, a shoplifter painted his face silver believing it would reflect the light and blur him on store cameras.
facts: Store cameras record continuously to hard drives
Silver body paint is worn by 'living statue' street performers
Shoplifting is the most common retail crime

truth.text: Under Swiss animal welfare law, it is strictly illegal to own only a single guinea pig because they are prone to loneliness.
facts: Part of Switzerland's 2008 animal protection rules
Guinea pigs are herd animals and get lonely
Other social pets, like budgies, need company too
A rental service lends a partner when one dies

lies.text: In Geneva, it is illegal to whistle on public trams after 10 p.m. under a 1950s noise ordinance.
facts: Geneva has had trams since 1862
Swiss towns enforce quiet hours, often after 10 p.m.
Switzerland has strict Sunday noise rules

truth.text: In France, it is legally permissible to marry a dead person under exceptional circumstances with presidential approval.
facts: Article 171 of the French Civil Code
Requires the president's approval and proof they meant to marry
Became known after a 1959 dam collapse killed a fiancé
Gives no inheritance rights; it's mostly symbolic

lies.text: In Ireland, it is illegal to sell potatoes on Good Friday under a 19th-century religious statute.
facts: Ireland's Great Famine (1845–52) was a potato crop failure
Pubs couldn't sell alcohol on Good Friday until 2018
Good Friday is the Friday before Easter

truth.text: In Ontario, Canada, the Apology Act of 2009 explicitly states that saying 'sorry' is not admissible in court as an admission of fault or liability.
facts: Lets people apologize without it being used against them
Covers civil cases, not criminal ones
Similar laws exist in British Columbia and many US states
Canadians are famous for apologizing reflexively

lies.text: In Australia, TV commercials featuring outdoor scenes must include at least one native plant species.
facts: Australia regulates ad content through industry codes
Eucalyptus and wattle are iconic native plants
Some countries set local-content quotas for TV

truth.text: Paris Syndrome is a recognised psychiatric condition where tourists suffer severe shock and hallucinations upon discovering Paris does not meet their romantic expectations.
facts: Named by Japanese psychiatrist Hiroaki Ota
Visitors expect romance, then meet rudeness and dirt
Culture shock and jet lag trigger anxiety and delusions
The Japanese embassy helps; some are flown home

lies.text: Kyoto Syndrome is a recognized condition where tourists overwhelmed by temple silence temporarily lose their voice.
facts: Kyoto has about 1,600 Buddhist temples
Temples ask visitors to keep quiet
Psychogenic voice loss is a real condition

truth.text: Cotard's Delusion is a rare neuropsychiatric condition where patients hold the delusion that they are dead, putrefying, or have lost their internal organs.
facts: Named after French neurologist Jules Cotard
Patients may claim they have no blood or organs
Linked to depression, psychosis and brain injury
Some stop eating, believing they don't need to

lies.text: Velvet Syndrome is a rare neurological condition where patients believe their skin has turned into fabric.
facts: Somatic delusions are false beliefs about one's own body
Delusional parasitosis makes people feel bugs under their skin
Tactile hallucinations make skin feel things that aren't there

truth.text: A neuroscientist cured excruciating phantom limb pain in amputees using an inexpensive mirror and optical illusion.
facts: The neuroscientist was V.S. Ramachandran
Many amputees feel pain in limbs that are gone
The patient hides the stump behind a mirror
Moving the real arm looks like the missing one moving
The brain 'unclenches' the phantom hand, easing the pain

lies.text: Staring at a blue light while eating lemons can make the sour taste noticeably milder.
facts: Color changes how food tastes in lab studies
Sourness comes from acids like citric acid
Blue is rare in natural foods

truth.text: Super Glue was accidentally discovered in 1942 while scientists were trying to synthesize crystal-clear plastic gun sights for Allied soldiers in WWII.
facts: Harry Coover at Kodak wanted clear plastic for gun sights
Cyanoacrylate stuck to everything, so it was rejected
Rediscovered in 1951 while developing jet canopies
Sold from 1958; used to close wounds in Vietnam

lies.text: Plastic wrap was originally invented in 1949 as a waterproof lining for soldiers' boots in cold climates.
facts: Plastic wrap is a thin film of PVC or polyethylene
Trench foot plagued soldiers in wet boots
Dow Chemical sold Saran Wrap from 1953

truth.text: Play-Doh was originally invented and marketed in the 1930s as a putty to clean coal soot off wallpaper.
facts: Kutol Products of Cincinnati made it to clean wallpaper
Coal heating left soot on walls
Gas heat and washable vinyl wallpaper killed sales
A teacher's class modeled with it; relaunched as a toy in 1956

lies.text: The garden hose was invented in 1870 by a fire brigade captain who wanted to water his roses with spare equipment.
facts: Early fire hoses were leather, riveted together
Rubber hoses became common in the late 1800s
Many fire brigades were volunteer-run in the 1800s

truth.text: The microwave oven was discovered when an engineer testing radar magnetrons noticed a peanut candy bar melted in his pocket.
facts: Percy Spencer at Raytheon, around 1945
Magnetrons made microwaves for wartime radar
He tested popcorn next; an egg exploded
The first 'Radarange' was nearly 6 feet tall

lies.text: The pop-up toaster was invented in 1909 by a Swiss watchmaker who adapted a clock spring as the timer.
facts: Electric toasters appeared in the early 1900s
Clock springs store energy to drive a timer
Switzerland was the center of watchmaking

truth.text: A DuPont chemist invented bulletproof Kevlar from a cloudy, watery liquid solution that her laboratory colleagues initially wanted to throw away.
facts: The chemist was Stephanie Kwolek
DuPont wanted a lighter, stronger fiber for tires
Her polymer solution was thin and cloudy, unlike the usual
She persuaded a technician to spin it into fiber
Now used in bulletproof vests, gloves and cables

lies.text: Velcro was originally designed in 1948 to fasten parachute harnesses for the Swiss air force.
facts: Hook-and-loop fasteners grip with tiny hooks and loops
Parachute harnesses use buckles and webbing straps
Switzerland stayed neutral in WWII

truth.text: Teflon was accidentally discovered when a chemist stored pressurized refrigerant gas in metal cylinders and opened them to find a slippery white powder.
facts: Roy Plunkett at DuPont, April 1938
The gas had polymerized inside the cylinder
First used for seals in the Manhattan Project
Non-stick pans came in the 1950s and 60s

lies.text: The zipper was originally engineered in 1893 as a fastener for horse-drawn carriage canopies.
facts: Whitcomb Judson showed a 'clasp locker' in 1893
Gideon Sundback turned it into the modern zipper
Carriage canopies were folding fabric covers

truth.text: Nicolas Cage outbid Leonardo DiCaprio at auction for a $276,000 dinosaur skull, only to discover it was illegally smuggled and return it to Mongolia.
facts: He bought a Tyrannosaurus bataar skull in 2007
It had been looted from Mongolia's Gobi Desert
US investigators traced it in 2014; Cage cooperated
He returned it and was never charged

lies.text: Actor Nicolas Cage once purchased an authentic 18th-century pirate cannon and mounted it in his home master bathroom.
facts: Cage once owned two castles and a pyramid tomb
Pirate ships carried cannons on wooden carriages
He later sold properties to settle tax debts

truth.text: In 2005, a 21-year-old student paid his university tuition by selling one million pixels on a blank webpage for $1 each.
facts: Alex Tew needed money for business school
Ads sold in 10×10 blocks for $100
The final 1,000 pixels sold on eBay for $38,100
Grossed about $1 million in five months

lies.text: In 2007, a British student paid for his degree by selling individual words in his dissertation's acknowledgments for £10 each.
facts: UK tuition fees rose to £3,000 a year in 2006
Acknowledgments thank people who helped with the work
Students have crowdfunded fees online

truth.text: The Japanese island of Tashirojima has an official feline population that outnumbers human residents by more than six to one.
facts: Villagers raised silkworms, and cats kept the mice away
Fishermen fed the cats and saw them as good luck
Dogs aren't allowed on the island
Has a cat shrine; under 100 mostly elderly residents

lies.text: In Norway, a small fjord island has 20 times more rabbits than people after a ferry captain released pets in the 1970s.
facts: Ōkunoshima in Japan really is overrun by rabbits
Rabbits breed fast, with litters of 4 to 12
Norway's coast has tens of thousands of small islands

truth.text: In 1980, Lake Peigneur in Louisiana completely drained away in hours after an oil drill accidentally pierced a massive salt mine below.
facts: Texaco was drilling for oil from a rig on the lake
The drill punctured the Diamond Crystal salt mine below
Water dissolved the salt, opening a huge whirlpool
All 55 miners escaped; the canal briefly ran backward

lies.text: In 1963, a lake in Idaho vanished overnight when an earthquake split an underwater fissure that redirected the water into an abandoned silver mine.
facts: Idaho's 1983 Borah Peak quake was magnitude 6.9
Northern Idaho's Silver Valley was a major silver district
Earthquakes can drain or create lakes by shifting ground

truth.text: The island nation of Vanuatu features a fully operational post office submerged three meters underwater in a marine sanctuary.
facts: Opened in 2003 off Hideaway Island
About three meters down in a marine reserve
Snorkelers buy waterproof postcards on shore
Staff dive down and emboss them with a special stamp

lies.text: In Iceland, a post office inside a lava tube cave stamps postcards with ink made from volcanic ash.
facts: Iceland has many lava tube caves, like Raufarhólshellir
Volcanic ash is fine, glassy rock dust
Postmarks are ink stamps showing the date and place

truth.text: An Italian real estate widow left her entire $13 million estate to a stray black cat named Tommaso.
facts: Owner Maria Assunta was a wealthy widow in Rome
She had taken Tommaso in as a stray
Italian law bars pets from inheriting directly

lies.text: A Texas oil billionaire left his 5,000-acre ranch to his three rescue donkeys, managed by a trust.
facts: US pet trusts can legally fund an animal's care
Hotelier Leona Helmsley left $12 million to her dog
Donkeys can live 30 to 50 years

truth.text: A Canadian lawyer's will bequeathed his vast fortune to whichever Toronto woman gave birth to the most children in a 10-year period.
facts: Charles Vance Millar loved practical jokes
His will set a ten-year baby race starting in 1926
It ran through the Great Depression, nicknamed the 'Stork Derby'
Four mothers with nine kids each split the prize

lies.text: A Chicago steel magnate's will offered his entire estate to any relative who could remain silent for an entire calendar year.
facts: Chicago was a steel hub with huge mills
Conditional wills set terms heirs must meet
Courts can void will conditions against public policy

truth.text: In 1859, a San Francisco resident declared himself 'Norton I, Emperor of the United States', and citizens treated him like royalty for 21 years.
facts: Joshua Norton lost his fortune trying to corner the rice market
He 'abolished' Congress and ordered a Bay bridge built
Local shops accepted his self-printed banknotes

lies.text: In 1910, a Boston blacksmith proclaimed himself Duke of New England and issued his own postage stamps that local shops accepted.
facts: Private 'local posts' issued stamps in 1800s US cities
Blacksmiths forged tools, horseshoes and hardware

truth.text: The inventor of the Pringles potato chip can was buried with his ashes placed inside a real Pringles can.
facts: Fredric Baur was a Procter & Gamble chemist

lies.text: The inventor of the Tupperware lid had his tombstone cast out of translucent yellow polyethylene resin.
facts: Earl Tupper founded Tupperware in 1946
Its airtight 'burping' seal was patented in 1949
